14 Abstract 15 Variations in noncoding regulatory sequences play a central role in evolution. 16 Interpreting such variations, however, remains difficult even in the context of defined 17 attributes such as transcription factor (TF) binding sites. Here, we systematically link 18 variations in cis-regulatory sequences to TF binding by profiling the allele-specific 19 binding of 27 TFs expressed in a yeast hybrid, in which two related genomes are present 20 within the same nucleus. TFs localize preferentially to sites containing their known 21 consensus motifs but occupy only a small fraction of the motif-coding sites available 22 within the genomes. Differential binding of TFs to the orthologous alleles was well 23 explained by variations that alter motif sequence, while differences in chromatin 24 accessibility between alleles were of little apparent effect. Motif variations that abolished 25 binding when present in one allele only, were still bound when present in both alleles, 26 suggesting evolutionary compensation, with a potential role for sequence conservation 27 at the motif’s vicinity. At the level of the full promoter, we identify cases of binding site 28 turnover, where binding sites are reciprocally gained and lost, yet most interspecific 29 differences remained uncompensated. Our results demonstrate the flexibility of TFs to 30 bind imprecise motifs and the fast evolution of TF binding sites between related species.
31 Introduction 32 Changes in gene expression play a key role in cellular adaptation, physiology and 33 development. Guiding these changes are transcription factors (TFs) that bind DNA at 34 sequence motifs allowing activation or repression of gene transcription. Understanding
1

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
35 how TF binding diverges between species is therefore central for understanding how 36 gene regulation evolves. 37 38 TFs contain DNA-binding domains (DBDs) that bind with high affinity to short DNA 39 sequence motifs (typically 6-12 base pairs). Sequence variations leading to the 40 emergence or disappearance of binding motifs may therefore drive regulatory 41 divergence by changing TF binding. Previous studies examined for such functional 42 variations by comparing TF binding between related species (Borneman et al., 2007; 43 Bradley et al., 2010; Paris et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2010; Stefflova et al., 2013; 44 Wilson et al., 2008), between human individuals (Kasowski et al., 2010; Kilpinen et al., 45 2013; Maurano et al., 2015) or between alleles of heterozygous cells (Reddy et al., 46 2012). It was proven difficult, however, to relate the measured changes in TF binding 47 with variations in motif sequence. In their analysis of allele-specific binding of 25 human 48 TFs, Reddy et al. concluded that only 12% of differentially-bound sites were associated 49 with variations in known binding sequences (Reddy et al., 2012). Similarly, studies 50 comparing binding of six TFs between two Drosophila species revealed only modest 51 correlation between inter-specific differences in binding and sequence variations in 52 known motifs (Bradley et al., 2010). 53 54 The difficulty of associating inter-species differences in TF binding with variations in cis55 regulatory sequences mirrors the difficulty in predicting TF binding sites. Indeed, motif 56 preference remains a poor indicator for TF binding in vivo, primarily because TFs 57 typically bind at only a small subset of motif-containing sites found in genomes. TF 58 binding could therefore evolve in cis not only through the emergence or disappearance 59 of binding motifs, but also through variations in DNA accessibility. Examples for such cis60 variations include changes in nucleosome positioning (Mirny, 2010; Sun et al., 2015), 61 variations affecting binding of a cooperating TF (Avsec et al., 2021; Stefflova et al., 62 2013), or variations in promoter regions surrounding the motif, perhaps recognized by 63 TF regions outside the DBD (Brodsky et al., 2020). 64 65 In this work, we systematically associated variations in known TF binding motifs to 66 changes in TF binding, by mapping allele-specific binding of 27 TFs within an inter67 specific yeast hybrid. The hybrid’s nucleus contains two related parental genomes. By 68 applying allele-specific mapping, we could directly compare TF binding to the two
2

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
69 genomes, while ensuring a uniform trans-regulatory environment (Emerson et al., 2010; 70 Floc’hlay et al., 2021; Hill et al., 2021; Krieger et al., 2020; Lupo et al., 2021; Metzger et 71 al., 2016; Tirosh et al., 2009; Wong et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021). Our analysis 72 examined the contribution of two types of variations, in sequence motifs and in 73 chromatin accessibility, to divergence of TF binding at individual binding sites. We 74 further examined evolutionary changes of TF binding at the full promoter level, by 75 distinguishing cases of compensated binding site turnover (in which loss of a binding site 76 is compensated by gain of an adjacent binding site) from cases of an uncompensated 77 gain/loss. Finally, by capitalizing on the hundreds of sequence variations in motif78 containing sites between the genomes, we defined the effective cost of each binding site 79 mutation in vivo, linking this cost with sequence conservation at the motif’s vicinity. Our 80 results highlight key aspects in the evolution of TF binding between closely related yeast 81 species. 82
83 Results
84 Mapping allele-specific binding of 27 transcription factors within an interspecies hybrid 85 86 To examine systematically the effect of cis variation on TF binding, we generated F1 87 hybrids by mating two closely related budding yeast species: S. cerevisiae and S. 88 paradoxus. These two species diverged approximately five million years ago, and largely 89 retained gene identity and synteny. Sequence identity reaches ~90% in coding regions 90 and ~75% in promoters (Scannell et al., 2011; Yue et al., 2017). Both species genomes 91 are highly compact with short intergenic regions (200 - 400 bp) that function primarily as 92 gene promoters. Others and us have previously used this hybrid as a model for studying 93 the principles of regulatory evolution (Artieri and Fraser, 2014; Emerson et al., 2010; 94 Krieger et al., 2020; Lupo et al., 2021; Metzger et al., 2016; Tirosh et al., 2009; Weiss et 95 al., 2018). 96 97 We selected 27 TFs of five protein families (Table S1). All selected TFs are of known 98 function, and their motif preferences were previously described through in vitro and in 99 vivo experiments (De Boer and Hughes, 2012; Sandelin et al., 2004). We mapped the 100 localization of these TFs along the orthologous hybrid genomes using chromatin 101 endonuclease cleavage followed by sequencing (ChEC-seq) (Zentner et al., 2015). For
3

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
102 this, each TF was fused to a MNase, allowing us to trigger DNA cleavage at the close 103 vicinity of the TF binding site using short (30 seconds) Ca2+ pulse. The short DNA 104 fragments were extracted and sequenced. We found this method to give a highly 105 reproducible and spatially-resolved TF binding maps (Bar-Ziv et al., 2020; Brodsky et al., 106 2020; Gera et al., 2021; Lupo et al., 2021). We previously observed that orthologous TF 107 proteins bind to similar locations in the hybrid genome and at a similar level, by profiling 108 both the S. cerevisiae TF orthologue and the S. paradoxus orthologue in separate 109 experiments (Lupo et al., 2021). This observation was consistent with the generally slow 110 evolution of TF preferences (Carroll, 2005). We therefore profiled only the S. cerevisiae 111 orthologue, examining how its binding differs between the two alleles (Figure 1 A). 112 Notably, comparing our binding profile with six published datasets revealed high 113 consistency in promoter binding, peak binding and preferred motifs (Supplemental note 114 1, Figure S16, Figure S17, Table S4, Table S5). Binding signals defined by ChEC-seq 115 were largely restricted to promoter regions, as expected (Figure S1 A). 116 117 Next, we compared TF binding between the two orthologues. For this, we distinguished 118 first the overall signal obtained throughout each promoter and second, the locations of 119 individual binding sites within promoters. Focusing first on the level of gene promoters, 120 we find high conservation: in all TFs, promoter binding pattern was correlated between 121 the two alleles (Pearson correlation coefficient, R, ranging from 0.75-0.96). Correlation 122 between experimental replicates was significantly higher (R ranging from 0.9 to 0.99), 123 supporting the reproducibility of our data, and suggesting that some allelic differences do 124 exist (Figure 1B). Of note, correlation between different TFs was much lower (Average R 125 = 0.12) (Figure S1 B). Other measures of correlation were also examined (Supplemental 126 note 3, Figure S 19); however, we found the Pearson linear correlation coefficient to be 127 most appropriate because most TFs bind a small number of targets. 128 129 Examining individual promoters, we noted various patterns of conservation and 130 divergence (Figure 1). In the case of Swi5, for example, promoter binding profiles were 131 highly similar between orthologues (R = 0.96), and this similarity extended when 132 examining binding peaks at highly bound promoters (e.g. SIC1, Figure 1C, experimental 133 replicates in Figure S1 C-E). In other cases, overall promoter binding was conserved 134 between the two alleles, yet the distribution of binding peaks varied along specific 135 promoters, implying on binding-site turnover (Dermitzakis and Clark, 2009; Ludwig et al.,
4

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
136 2000; Moses et al., 2006). For example, Tbf1 showed similar overall binding to the 137 CTH1/GIR2 promoter in the two orthologous alleles, yet, the precise binding pattern 138 differed, and this variation was linked to a change in the location of the Tbf1 motif within 139 the two orthologous promoters (Figure 1 D, blue box). We also observed cases of 140 divergence, in which overall binding differed between the two orthologous promoters, as 141 exemplified by the binding of Reb1 to the GSP2 promoter, which was significantly 142 stronger at the S. paradoxus allele. Also here, differential binding correlated with the 143 presence of an additional Reb1 motif in S. paradoxus allele but not in the S. cerevisiae 144 allele (Figure 1 E). We conclude that while TF binding remains largely invariant at the 145 resolution of the full promoter, cases of cis divergence at the level of individual TF 146 binding sites are readily identified. 147 148 149
150 Transcription factors bind a selected subset of motif-containing sites within the two 151 genomes 152 153 Promoter regions in budding yeast are typically 200 - 400 base pairs (bp) long (Figure S 154 1 F, Kristiansson et al., 2009), while individual binding sites contain only 6-12 bp. To 155 examine whether our data can define TF binding at a resolution that is compatible with 156 individual binding sites, we first observed the binding signal around motif-containing sites 157 (Figure 2 A), referring to the known in vitro motif of each TF as curated in the YetFasco 158 (De Boer and Hughes, 2012) and JASPAR (Sandelin et al., 2004) databases. For most 159 TFs, these in vitro defined motifs agreed well with de novo motifs defined from our data 160 by either enrichment of 7-mer sequences around bound sites or the MEME-ChIP 161 algorithm (Machanick and Bailey, 2011) (Table S1, Supplemental note 1). 162 163 Considering first the Reb1 TF, we find binding signal at locations containing its in vitro 164 motif, as expected. Binding, however, was restricted to only ~30% of motif sites found 165 within promoters (Figure 2 A). In this analysis, we estimated the significance of TF 166 binding relative to a set of random sites within promoters and defined a binding threshold 167 at 95% of random site distribution (Figure 2 B), resulting in 2063 Reb1-bound sites. 168 Binding level at motif sites was moderately correlated (R = 0.25) with the motif p-value 169 as defined by FIMO (Grant et al., 2011). Consistent with the expected pattern of this
5

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
170 method, MNase-cleavage signal peaked at the motif boundaries and was depleted from 171 within the motif itself, the latter is protected from cleavage by the bound TF (Figure 2 A). 172 Results for other TFs were similar, although varied in details depending on TF identity: 173 such as the cleavage symmetry around the motif and the width of the cleavage174 protected region (Figure 2 C, full profiles in Figure S2). These details perhaps reflect 175 differences in TF mobility on the DNA (Suter, 2020), motif-specificity and the size of the 176 protein or protein-complex bound to the DNA. An example for the latter factor may be 177 Hap4, where the protected area appears significantly larger (30 bases) than the known 178 motif (7 bases) (Figure 2 C), perhaps indicating its binding as a subunit of the larger 179 Hap2/3/4/5 transcriptional activation complex (McNabb and Pinto, 2005). We conclude 180 that ChEC-seq allows mapping of individual binding locations with high resolution. 181 182 To map individual binding sites we used an available peak-calling algorithm (Materials 183 and methods). Peak locations were largely consistent with previously published data 184 (Supplemental note 1, Figure S16). Notably, a considerable fraction (0.2 – 0.6) of reads 185 were mapped to peaks (Figure S4). Overall, 28% of the peaks were associated with the 186 known in vitro motif, here referred to as binding sites, in which peaks and motifs are less 187 than 30 bases apart (Figure S5 A). The percentage of peaks associated with the known 188 in vitro motifs (all motif realizations with FIMO p-value < 0.001) ranged from 8% to 62% 189 between the different TFs. This fraction was 2.5 times higher than the fraction of random 190 sites that reside next to an in vitro motif (averaging over all TFs), resembling high motif191 association of peaks in our data. We observe high specificity of TFs to their binding 192 sites, with low overlap between TFs (2% - 4%, Figure S18 D) and no typical binding 193 pattern at binding sites of an unrelated TF (Figure S3). 194 195 To estimate the level of systematic noise in our data, namely binding peaks that are not 196 due to TF binding, we tested the ChEC-seq profile of an endogenously expressed free197 MNase (Supplemental note 2, Figure S18). Only 2.5% - 4% of TF binding peaks 198 overlapped with free-MNase peaks, representing the false-positive rate of the method 199 and agreeing with previous estimations (Zentner et al., 2015). Therefore, the high 200 number of peaks that were not motif-associated, were also not bound by a free-MNase, 201 and may indicate functional binding events. Such events might result for example, from 202 recruitment by interacting TF, or from protein regions outside the DBD that interact with 203 DNA. As the sequence basis of these binding events is not characterized, we decided to
6

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
204 focus our analysis on binding peaks containing the known in vitro motifs, representing 205 8% to 62% of TF-specific peaks (Figure S5 A). 206 207
208 Differential TF binding to the two hybrid alleles correlates with variations in motif 209 sequence, while differences in motif accessibility play a minor role 210 211 TFs could gain new binding sites through at least two mechanisms (Figure 3 A). First, 212 mutations could change the accessibility of the DNA in regions containing a motif site, 213 for example through sequence mutations causing a nucleosome-depleted region. 214 Second, new motifs could emerge by mutations within accessible region. As these two 215 processes occur in parallel, their prevalence may vary depending on the motif type and 216 the processes governing TF specificity, namely its attraction to only a subset of its motif217 containing sites. 218 219 To distinguish between these two mechanisms of divergence, we focused on TF binding 220 to motif-containing sites. To enable comparison of orthologous binding sites, we locally 221 aligned orthologous promoters, and compared sequence and binding level over the 222 aligned coordinates (materials and methods). We distinguish between sites where both 223 orthologues contain the corresponding motif (conserved between species; common) and 224 sites where the motif is found in only one species’ genome (diverged between species; 225 unique). Overall, 36% of sites were classified as common sites, 36% as cerevisiae226 unique, and 27% as paradoxus-unique (Figure 3 B, Figure S6 A). As expected, the 227 fraction of common sites bound by the respective TFs was, on average, twice as high as 228 that of the unique sites (Figure S6 B). 229 230 A significant fraction of common sites remained unbound in both genomes, implying that 231 these sites are likely to be inaccessible for TF binding (Figure 3 B, Figure S6 C). Indeed, 232 for most TFs (e.g. Reb1), nucleosome occupancy at unbound sites was higher than that 233 at bound ones (Figure 3 C, Figure S7), while other TFs (e.g. the stress-related TF Sok2) 234 were preferentially bound at sites that are often nucleosome-occupied, as reported 235 before (Kaplan et al., 2009). On average, most TF were preferentially bound at sites of 236 low nucleosome occupancy, prompting us to ask whether changes in nucleosome 237 occupancy between alleles could also explain the divergence of binding. For this, we
7

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
238 asked whether cases in which both orthologous alleles contain a motif (common motif), 239 yet only one of these alleles is in fact bound, might result from differential nucleosome 240 occupancy of the two alleles. We find that in these cases, and also in cases of unique 241 motif sites, nucleosomes are equally positioned in the bound and non-bound orthologues 242 (Figure 3 C, Figure S7). This suggests that the differences in DNA accessibility, at least 243 as reflected by nucleosome occupancy, play a minor role in the divergence of TF binding 244 preferences. 245 246 To examine whether differential TF binding correlates with the emergence or loss of the 247 binding motif, we focused on cases of unique sites, in which the motif is present in only 248 one of the alleles. We asked whether, in these cases, the allele containing the motif is 249 more likely to be bound than the one that lacks the motif. This was indeed the case 250 (Figure 3 D): in 25/27 TF in our set, we observed high correspondence between the 251 allele containing the motif and the one bound by the respective TFs. Together, these 252 data suggest that divergence in TF binding due to changes in DNA accessibility are less 253 frequent compared to these caused by the emergence or loss of a binding motif. 254
255 TF binding to an imperfect motif depends on the genomic context 256 257 Our analysis so far focused on cases where TF binding was lost or gained in one of the 258 genomes. Next, we considered also quantitative changes, where TFs bound the two 259 alleles but at different levels. Such quantitative differences in the allele-specific TF 260 binding were in fact quite common and accounted for the majority of binding changes 261 (Figure S8). We asked whether these quantitative differences could be explained by 262 sequence variations within the binding motif. For this, we focused on binding peaks that 263 contain the associated motif in at least one of the genome, and considered the sequence 264 variations within the motif site and in its immediate surroundings. To further focus the 265 analysis, we considered first cases of unique alternative alleles, in which one orthologue 266 has the consensus motif (as defined in vitro), while the second orthologue has a one267 letter variant either within the motif itself, or in its flanking region (five bases upstream / 268 downstream the core motif). Comparing TF binding occupancy at the two orthologues 269 allowed quantifying the average cost (reduction in TF binding) of each deviation from 270 consensus (Figure 4 A). 271
8

Downloaded from genome.cshlp.org on May 29, 2022 - Published by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press
272 For Reb1, deviations from consensus in the core motif had a strong impact on binding 273 (Figure 4 A). This sensitivity to deviation from the consensus motif differed between TFs 274 and was further dependent on the position and the precise alternative (Figure 4 C). In 275 fact, some TFs remained largely insensitive to single-letter variations (e.g. Skn7, Gcr2, 276 Stb3), while others showed greatly reduced binding (e.g. Rap1, Tbf1, Pho4). In some 277 cases, variations in sequences flanking the known motif were also of apparent 278 consequences: in the case of Reb1, for example, a “T” at position -1 was associated with 279 100 folds reduction in binding (Figure 4 A). Of note, Reb1 protein was shown to bind the 280 DNA base at the -1 position, and a “T” at that position was predicted to distort DNA 281 shape (Jaiswal et al., 2016; Rossi et al., 2018). This effect outside of the core motif, 282 however, was the exception, as in most cases, variants of apparent effect were 283 restricted to the motif itself, suggesting little contribution from the immediate motif284 flanking region. 285 286 Our analysis therefore supports the notion that sequence variations within the known cis 287 regulatory motif reduce binding in a manner that depends on the TF and the precise 288 sequence alternative. We next asked whether these same deviations from the 289 consensus motif exert a similar cost on binding also when conserved in both species’ 290 genomes (common alternative). 475 Understanding the sequence determinants of transcription factor binding in living cells is 476 a major challenge. In this study, we profiled in vivo TF binding in a yeast hybrid that 477 contains two related genomes within the same nucleus. The high sequence divergence 478 in regulatory regions between these two genomes (~25%) provides a wide range of 479 sequence variation that can be examined in parallel. This enabled us to measure how 480 multitudes of sequence variations affect TF binding within a genomic context. 481 482 Differential binding can result from differential use of a common pool of potential binding 483 sites containing the binding motif, or from gain/loss of sequence motifs. Our data 484 supports the second scenario, as we found that most conserved motif sites were either 485 bound or unbound in both genomes, while differentially bound sites were associated with 486 a sequence variation within the binding motifs. Further, we detected little, if any, 487 differences in nucleosome positioning at sites that are differentially bound. Therefore in 488 yeast, sequence evolution in regulatory regions appears to occur more readily than 489 changes in chromatin accessibility at TF binding sites, in agreement with previous 490 studies (Tirosh et al., 2010; Tsankov et al., 2010). The ability of a TF to bind its motif491 containing site was also shown to depend on DNA shape features (Abe et al., 2015; 492 Zhou et al., 2015), however these features did not separate between in vivo bound and 493 unbound motif-containing sites (Zentner et al., 2015) and therefore were not examined in 494 this study. 495 496 TFs bind strongly at sites containing their consensus motif, compatible with sequence 497 motifs defined in vitro. We expected to observe binding also at sites containing imprecise 498 motifs, for example sites containing one alternative base, but that this binding would be, 499 on average, lower than binding to the consensus motif. This was indeed the case when 500 an alternative base was present in one allele only, while the second allele carried the 501 consensus motif. Notably, however, we find that genomic sites containing the same 502 alternative allele in both orthologous genomes were bound at almost the same extent as 503 sites containing the consensus motif. A perfect consensus sequence might not always 504 be the best for the organism in terms of fitness at each site, however. Non-consensus, or 505 low-affinity binding sites are in fact widespread in the yeast genome (Tanay, 2006), and 506 were shown to be important in fly and mouse development (Crocker et al., 2016; Rowan 507 et al., 2010; Scardigli et al., 2003). 508

509 We have further shown that imprecise (weak) motifs of certain TFs, which appear in both 510 orthologous alleles, commonly reside in regions of exceptionally high sequence 511 conservation. This observation is in contrast to the cases of consensus sites, which are 512 often found as islands of conservation within sequence-diverged regions. This may be 513 related to a previous report showing that polymorphisms in CTCF motifs have greater 514 effects on TF binding when they appear in sequence-diverged regions than in sequence515 conserved regions (Spivakov et al., 2012). The authors attribute this effect to co-factors 516 that allow CTCF to bind at imprecise motifs. In our case, such binding partners are 517 known for Rap1 (Tornow et al., 1993) but have not been described for the other TFs. We 518 find it more likely that this effect is related to chromatin, as the TFs showing this effect 519 (Abf1, Reb1 and Rap1) all act in the regulation of nucleosome positioning (Rhee and 520 Pugh, 2011). Therefore, we speculate that the presence of other TFs at nearby sites 521 stabilizes the binding of these TFs to non-optimal motif sites (Mirny, 2010). Another 522 possibility involves DNA interactions through the non-DNA-binding domain parts of the 523 protein (Brodsky et al., 2020). To conclude, we suggest that non-consensus sites are 524 bound to a high level and are species-conserved due to a local sequence compensation. 525 526 In the majority of the TFs we examined, variability in binding to the two orthologues was 527 well explained by sequence variation in the motif and its immediate surroundings. 528 Previous studies addressing the problem of predicting binding variation from sequence 529 variation, reported on a generally limited predicting power for differential TF binding 530 (Bradley et al., 2010; Halow et al., 2021; He et al., 2011b; Reddy et al., 2012; Stefflova 531 et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2010). In an influential study for the field, Reddy et al. 532 measured TF binding of in human heterozygous cell lines, and reported that only 12% of 533 differentially-bound sites were associated with sequence variations in known binding 534 motifs (Reddy et al., 2012). Here, we report a similar fraction (19%), however, when 535 considering only motif-associated peaks, we find that most (60%) of the differentially 536 bound sites were associated with a sequence variation in the motif. Further, using 537 quantitative models, we show that variability in motif score is the best predictor for 538 variability in TF binding, whereby other features had limited contribution. Our improved 539 prediction may result from the use of the ChEC-seq method which provides high540 resolution mapping of TF binding. In addition, the use of F1 hybrids for this work allows 541 profiling both orthologous genomes in the same cell and thus reduces both technical and 542 trans-driven variations that can reduce power and hamper interspecific comparisons.

543 544 When classifying evolutionary changes in TF binding at the promoter level, we find that 545 most of the bound promoters involve unbalanced gain or loss of binding sites, whereas 546 only 7% of the bound promoters show evidence of compensation by binding site 547 turnover. This result is in agreement with reports from other model organisms, including 548 the Zeste TF in Drosophila (Moses et al., 2006), liver-specific TFs in mice (Stefflova et 549 al., 2013) and individual TFs in yeast (Borneman et al., 2007). Furthermore, higher rates 550 of positive and purifying selection compared to compensatory neutral evolution were 551 modeled for Drosophila enhancers (He et al., 2011a), but not for yeast promoters 552 (Mustonen et al., 2008). The flexibility and high rate of binding site evolution suggests 553 that in many cases binding site loss or addition is not deleterious. Overall, we find that 554 TF binding evolves through gains and losses of binding sites, with quantitative changes 555 in binding level being highly predictable from sequence variation within the motif. 556 557 To conclude, in this study we report on two linked observations: 1) imprecise but 558 conserved motifs are bound to a high level by TFs, and 2) the observation of short559 distance binding sites turnover, where binding localization is conserved despite of 560 sequence divergence. These observations demonstrate the fast and flexible evolution of 561 TF binding sites between related species, and we expect to see these phenomena in 562 other organisms as well. 563

RESEARCH ARTICLES
First release: 29 May 2025 science.org (Page numbers not final at time of first release) 1
The precise control of gene expression is broadly important across human health and development, but the mechanisms by which genomic sequence encodes these intricate programs remain incompletely understood. Central to gene regulation is the promoter, the site of transcriptional initiation, which integrates signals across multiple non-coding sequence elements to determine the proper cellular and temporal context for turning genes on and off. Experimental studies of promoters have shown that they can dramatically increase or decrease gene expression (1), suggesting that non-coding variants which fall within the promoters of clinically relevant genes may play key roles in rare genetic disorders and cancer (2, 3). However, clinical interest in promoter variants has been limited, due to the difficulty of distinguishing between functional non-coding variants that affect gene expression and those that are neutral, with only a handful of pathogenic non-coding variants in promoters having been identified to date (4–12). These challenges in finding pathogenic variants that lie outside protein-coding sequence continue to be a
major hindrance to realizing the potential of personalized genome sequencing. Deep learning models, known for their efficacy at recognizing patterns from large volumes of unstructured data, offer a promising path forward for distilling data collected from genome-wide sequencing and functional genomics experiments into models that can accurately predict the clinical impact of human genetic variation (13, 14). Recent examples that have seen adoption in clinical contexts include SpliceAI (15), which has been cited in expert guidelines for splice variant effect prediction in rare genetic disorders and oncology (16), and missense variant prediction based on protein language models and 3D crystal structures (PrimateAI-3D) (17). While deep learning models such as Evo2 (18), DeepSEA (19), Basenji (20), ExPecto (21), Enformer (22), PuffinD (23), ChromBPNet (24), and Borzoi (25) have been developed to infer the regulatory code directly from genomic sequence, predicting the effects of non-coding genetic variants remains an unmet challenge (26, 27).

Only a minority of patients with rare genetic diseases are currently diagnosed by exome sequencing, suggesting that additional unrecognized pathogenic variants may reside in non-coding sequence. Here, we describe PromoterAI, a deep neural network that accurately identifies non-coding promoter variants which dysregulate gene expression. We show that promoter variants with predicted expression-altering consequences produce outlier expression at both RNA and protein levels in thousands of individuals, and that these variants experience strong negative selection in human populations. We observe that clinically relevant genes in rare disease patients are enriched for such variants and validate their functional impact through reporter assays. Our estimates suggest that promoter variation accounts for 6% of the genetic burden associated with rare diseases.

Results
PromoterAI predicts the effects of promoter variants on gene expression
We introduce PromoterAI, a convolutional deep neural network model that uses ~20 kb of sequence context around a promoter variant to predict its expression consequence. We first trained the model to predict histone modifications, DNA accessibility, transcription factor (TF) occupancy, and strandspecific CAGE [Cap Analysis of Gene Expression (28, 29)] values around transcription start sites (TSS) at base-pair resolution. We subsequently fine-tuned the model using a curated set of rare non-coding promoter variants associated with unusually high or low gene expression to further improve its accuracy across extensive validation benchmarks, which we publish as a resource (Fig. 1A, fig. S1A, and table S1, A to G). To create this curated list of variants for fine-tuning, we analyzed the Genotype-Tissue Expression v8 (GTEx) cohort, consisting of paired whole genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA-seq data across 49 tissues in 838 individuals (30). Specifically, we cataloged a set of rare (allele frequency < 0.5%) variants in the promoters of genes (TSS +/− 500 bp) with outlier expression across multiple tissues. These multi-tissue outliers were identified via a t-test between expression zscores from all measured tissues in the carriers versus the same tissues in non-carriers. To maximize confidence in the resulting outliers, when generating the expression z-scores, we subtracted out the contribution of other factors that also affect gene expression: principal components from the expression and genotype matrices, cis-effects of common expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) on gene expression, and trans-effects of correlated patterns of gene expression (Fig. 1B). To perform the trans-expression correction, we predicted each gene’s expression using the expression of all genes residing on other chromosomes and then subtracted the predicted expression values from the observed values, since these generally reflect global patterns unrelated to the effects of promoter sequence. To assess the gain in specificity after each correction step, we compared the number of observed expression outliers to background expectation, which we estimated by shuffling the cohort with variants being randomly re-assigned between individuals. After initially correcting for genotype and expression principal components, we found 2,540 multi-tissue outliers at a p-value threshold that produced 1,000 outliers in the shuffled controls; this increased to 3,116 after correcting for cis-eQTLs, and finally to 4,030 following the trans-expression correction (Fig. 1B and table S2). Individuals whose observed gene expression deviated from their predicted gene expression were enriched up to 6-fold for carrying a rare promoter variant in that gene for under-expression, and 2.5-fold for overexpression (Fig. 1C). To identify the extent of the region surrounding the TSS where we can robustly identify multi-tissue expression
outliers, we calculated enrichments of variants with significant effects on gene expression (t-test, p < 1e-4) within 100 bp sliding windows at distances up to 5 kb from the TSS (Fig. 1D). This analysis revealed that expression outliers were predominantly located within 500 bp upstream and downstream of the TSS. While these enrichments improved when the analysis was restricted to conserved promoters (fig. S1B), selecting the most frequently used TSS across tissues was critical for maximizing enrichments (fig. S1C and table S3). We benchmarked our approach against other existing methods to quantify aberrant expression, including an unsupervised autoencoder model from OUTRIDER (31), and two summary statistics available from GTEx (32): median z-scores across tissues and median p-values from an allelic imbalance test (ANEVA-DOT) (33). Compared to the other methods, when choosing thresholds that result in the same false discovery rate in shuffled controls, our approach detected greater enrichment of multi-tissue outliers (Fig. 1E). Using allele-specific expression to assess variants with phasing data available, we found that alleles carrying overexpression outliers had significantly higher allelic expression compared to alleles carrying under-expression outliers (p = 7.4e-29; fig. S1D). As a further orthogonal validation, we observed that the proportion of promoter variants with either over- or under-expression effects was highest for positions with high constraint across 470 mammals (phyloP-470 way; Fig. 1F), indicating that both types of outliers disproportionately fall within conserved sequence elements. Next, we used multi-tissue outliers, as well as matched control variants that came from the promoters of the same genes but showed no effects on expression, and trained PromoterAI on the variants from the odd chromosomes (see Methods for details), while variants from the even chromosomes were set aside for testing and evaluating the model. We benchmarked PromoterAI, Evo2, DeepSEA, Basenji, ExPecto, Enformer, PuffinD, ChromBPNet, and Borzoi on three variant classification tasks, namely, under- vs overexpression, under-expression vs control variants that did not affect gene expression (null), and overexpression vs null (Fig. 1G, left). PromoterAI performed the best out of these models across all three metrics by achieving an auROC of 0.89, 0.80, and 0.74, respectively. We also benchmarked the performance of each classifier on multiple massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) saturation mutagenesis datasets, including the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation (CAGI5) dataset, where we focused on promoters of disease-associated genes (3), and another dataset comprising promoters with known eQTLs and hits from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (34). PromoterAI achieved the best performance (Fig. 1G, right, and fig. S1E) and also demonstrated strong per-gene predictive capability, as evidenced by correlations between model scores and MPRA effect sizes calculated

Under- and overexpression variants primarily act by disrupting motifs
To understand the basis of PromoterAI’s predictions, we systematically performed in-silico mutagenesis in the vicinity of GTEx outliers, using only the variants from the even chromosomes that were set aside for testing and evaluating the model. Consistent with the model learning the underlying biological mechanisms, PromoterAI assigned high scores to variants that disrupted the motifs of TFs with widely known effects on gene expression, with several representative examples shown (Fig. 2A and fig. S2A). Under-expression variants were particularly enriched for disrupting ETS motifs (Fig. 2B), recognized to be involved in a wide range of regulatory processes (35), along with YY1, ATF1, and NRF1 motifs, which are known to have broad regulatory functions at promoters (36–39). In contrast, overexpression outliers were enriched for disrupting E2F motifs (Fig. 2B), which have roles in cell cycle control and tumor suppression (40), alongside other transcriptional families such as NFKB, INSM1, ERR-alpha, and TFAP2 (41–44). We inserted these motifs along the lengths of promoters to assess their effects using PromoterAI and found that the predictions were consistent with the evidence from expression outliers (fig. S2B), while also localizing the optimal region for maximal effect to 100 bp immediately upstream and downstream of the TSS (45). These in-silico experiments reinforce that PromoterAI successfully learns sequence determinants of promoter regulation. We further examined the relative contributions of variants that affect gene expression by strengthening or weakening motifs, using a curated list of motifs (table S4) exclusively associated with activating or repressive Gene Ontology (GO) terms (46). We found that under-expression outliers were enriched for weakening of motifs associated with only activating GO terms (Fig. 2C, left). In contrast, overexpression outliers were enriched for both weakening of motifs associated with only repressive GO terms and, to a lesser extent, strengthening of motifs associated with only activating GO terms (Fig. 2C, right). Similar trends were observed for motifs associated with both activating and repressive GO terms, subcategorized based on their relative proportions, although the effects were less pronounced due to the complexity of these motifs (fig. S2C). Our results show that it is generally easier for newly occurring variants to cause outlier gene expression by disrupting existing regulatory components rather than creating new ones, as well as highlighting the important role of transcriptional repressors in promoter regulation. Next, we investigated the contribution of fine-tuning to PromoterAI’s performance, aiming to discern the specific variant types which saw the largest gains. We first stratified expression outliers by the motifs they overlapped, and
calculated the correlation between the actual and predicted effects of variants before and after fine-tuning. We saw substantial improvement in performance across nearly all motifs (Fig. 2D) as well as across TSS distance (fig. S2D). We also repeated the earlier analysis of inserting motifs along the lengths of promoters, using the models before and after finetuning. We observed that the predicted direction of effect aligned more consistently with the evidence from expression outliers after fine-tuning (fig. S2E), suggesting that fine-tuning may overcome limitations in predicting the directionality of motifs which has been highlighted in recent papers (26, 27). Moreover, we found that the nucleotide positions which experienced the largest differences in PromoterAI scores before and after fine-tuning tended to be highly conserved (Fig. 2E). Given that conservation information was not used during training or fine-tuning, these results provide independent evidence suggesting that fine-tuning with expression outliers enables the model to more effectively learn the underlying causal biological mechanisms. We show representative examples where fine-tuning led to substantial changes in PromoterAI predictions, noting that the model before fine-tuning frequently recognized the underlying motif but predicted the direction of effect incorrectly (Fig. 2F and fig. S2F). In order to investigate PromoterAI’s internal representations of promoter biology, we extracted feature embeddings of all canonical promoters of protein-coding genes, finding that they clustered into three distinct classes (fig. S3A and table S5): a first class of 9,234 genes abundantly expressed across most tissues and enriched for activating histone marks and ubiquitously expressed TFs, a second class of 3,430 genes characterized by bivalent chromatin, and a third class of 6,632 genes with mainly tissue-specific expression and enriched for repressive histone marks (fig. S3, B to F) (47). The three classes also differed in expression variability, with the first class resembling low-variability promoters, while the second and third classes resembled highly variable promoters (48). Observing that the third promoter class bears many enhancer-like characteristics (49), we used PromoterAI to extract feature embeddings from distal enhancers and compared them with those from promoters. Indeed, the feature embeddings of distal enhancers closely resembled those of the third promoter class (fig. S3G). This enhancer-like promoter class was notably depleted for conserved elements, further emphasizing its distinct regulatory properties (fig. S3H).
Promoter variants that impact gene expression are under strong negative selection
To measure the extent of negative selection acting on promoter variants in human populations, we turned to the Genome Aggregation Database v3 (gnomAD) cohort (50, 51), which includes whole genome sequencing data from 71,702 individuals. We used PromoterAI to score each promoter

variant, excluding those with protein-coding or splicing effects, and compared the number of predicted expression-altering variants at common allele frequencies (> 0.1%) to rare singletons. We based our analysis on the observation that natural selection purges deleterious variants over time, preventing them from becoming widespread in the population (50, 52).
Variants predicted by PromoterAI to alter gene expression were strongly depleted of common variants relative to rare variants, indicating that expression-altering variants are being actively removed by natural selection (Fig. 3A). This depletion applied to both predicted under- and overexpression variants and became more pronounced with increasing magnitude of PromoterAI scores. At PromoterAI scores near +0.5 or -0.5, the observed depletion approached that of missense variants, while scores closer to +1 or -1 resulted in a depletion percentage comparable to that of nonsense variants. We further stratified genes by evolutionary constraint, as measured by probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) (52). We observed a greater depletion for expression-altering variants in the promoters of high pLI genes, consistent with these genes being dosage sensitive and associated with haploinsufficient disease mechanisms (Fig. 3B). We also stratified variants by TSS distance, dividing the promoter region into 10 bp non-overlapping windows and estimating the number of singleton variants expected to be depleted by natural selection in each window (Fig. 3C). Similar to expression outliers being enriched near the TSS, the depletion signal also peaked in a region within 100 bp of the TSS, with a notably stronger signal for under-expression than overexpression variants, suggesting that under-expression variants tend to be more deleterious on average.
PromoterAI accurately predicts the effects of finemapped promoter eQTLs
We assessed PromoterAI’s ability to predict the effects of finemapped GTEx eQTLs. For this, we identified 409 eQTLs that mapped to a single variant with posterior probability > 0.9 in multiple tissues using CAVIAR (53), after excluding splice variants, protein-coding variants, and GTEx rare variants that were used for fine-tuning, which we followed in all subsequent benchmarking analyses. PromoterAI scores were significantly correlated with the observed eQTL effect sizes (r = 0.56, p = 8.2e-36; Fig. 3D, left), and variants that were predicted to cause under- or overexpression showed nearly nonoverlapping effect size distributions (p = 6.0e-37; Fig. 3D, middle). Next, we compared PromoterAI’s performance at classifying eQTLs to other classifiers. For this, we included 393 control promoter eQTLs from the same genes as the finemapped eQTLs, focusing on those that were not prioritized by fine-mapping (posterior probability < 0.1 in all tissues). For each of the three classification tasks, namely
distinguishing under-expression eQTLs vs overexpression eQTLs, under-expression eQTLs vs control variants, and overexpression eQTLs vs control variants, PromoterAI’s auROC was 0.87, 0.79, and 0.75, respectively, exceeding the performance of other classifiers (Fig. 3D, right). We note that the lower auROC values in this task reflect that the statistical fine-mapping procedure includes a degree of uncertainty in the assignment of the fine-mapped causal variant due to linkage disequilibrium. We leveraged recently generated MPRA data for these eQTLs (34), which directly assays the effects of fine-mapped variants in cell culture, and avoids the limitations posed by linkage disequilibrium (54). We found a robust correlation of 0.63 (p = 6.1e-77) between PromoterAI scores and measured effect sizes across 686 promoter eQTLs (Fig. 3E, left). We calculated the validation rates across the range of PromoterAI scores, defined as the proportion of variants with effect size in the assay exceeding the recommended cutoffs of -0.5 or +0.5. Validation rates increased monotonically with PromoterAI scores along both directions, with nearly all variants predicted to have large effects validating successfully in the assay (Fig. 3E, middle). We used the MPRA dataset as an additional benchmark to test each classifier’s performance at distinguishing between overexpression, under-expression, and null variants, with PromoterAI showing the best results (Fig. 3E, right; 0.90, 0.81, 0.83, respectively, as measured by auROC).

Expression-altering promoter variants are enriched in patients with rare genetic disorders
Large-scale sequencing studies of patients with rare genetic diseases have found that pathogenic protein-coding variants can be identified in fewer than half of these patients, leaving the rest without a definitive genetic diagnosis (58, 59). To investigate the extent to which non-coding variants are potentially contributing to rare diseases, we applied PromoterAI to score singleton variants in the promoters of known rare disease genes for patients in the Genomics England (GEL) cohort (60). We counted the number of times PromoterAI predicted an expression-altering variant in a gene that was
specific to the patient’s disease, based on gene panels annotated by the Genomics England PanelApp database for each rare disease (Fig. 5A) (61, 62). To estimate background expectation for such matches to occur by chance, we shuffled the cohort 100 times, each time randomly re-assigning variants to each individual. We focused on a set of 7,948 probands with no already prioritized variant (TIER1), and with fewer than 100 causative genes in their disease gene panels to limit noise and the likelihood of spurious matches (fig. S4, D and E). Rare heterozygous variants predicted to cause under-expression by PromoterAI (score < -0.05) were significantly enriched in genes specific to patients’ disease compared to shuffled controls (1.3x, p = 3e-4, n = 188). This enrichment increased when restricting to genes with autosomal dominant inheritance pattern (1.5x, p = 1e-5, n = 138), and further increased when restricting to genes with a loss-of-function mechanism (1.6x, p = 2e-4, n = 84; Fig. 5, A and B) (63), consistent with these variants causing disease through a haploinsufficiency mechanism. To ensure that these variants reflected non-coding regulatory effects, we excluded missense, protein-truncating, and splice variants while calculating enrichments (fig. S4F). We estimated diagnostic yield using the number of observed variants minus the expected number seen in shuffled controls across different variant categories (Fig. 5C). Overall, within this rare genetic disease cohort, we estimate that promoter variants account for 6% of the total diagnostic yield, which when combined with the 14% attributable to cryptic splice variants (SpliceAI > 0.2), implies that non-coding variants account for roughly 1 in 5 cases (Fig. 5D). As an additional control, we included synonymous variants and missense variants that were classified as benign (PrimateAI3D < 0.2) and found that neither of these variant types showed significant enrichment compared to the randomly shuffled background. We did not observe a significant enrichment for predicted overexpression variants in the annotated genes from PanelApp (fig. S4G). Given the evidence for their deleteriousness in human populations as indicated by their depletion in the gnomAD cohort, overexpression promoter variants may account for additional rare genetic disease cases, but with different genes and phenotypes than proteincoding variants. We assessed PromoterAI’s predictions using whole blood RNA-seq data from 4,949 predominantly undiagnosed rare disease patients in the GEL cohort. PromoterAI scores in these probands were robustly correlated with changes in gene expression in blood RNA-seq (r = 0.61, p = 6.6e-171; Fig. 5E, left), and the majority of variants with PromoterAI scores > 0.5 or < -0.5 tended to alter gene expression by at least 2 standard deviations in the predicted direction (Fig. 5E, middle). Discussion
Non-coding genetic variants account for the vast majority of genome-wide associations for common diseases (75, 76), but their role in rare genetic diseases is only beginning to be defined. In a diverse rare disease cohort, we demonstrate that promoters of disease-relevant genes are enriched for PromoterAI-predicted expression-altering variants and provide further evidence of their functional impact through MPRA experiments, suggesting that promoter variation may account for a meaningful fraction of cases not previously

attributed to coding variation. A crucial factor driving PromoterAI’s effectiveness compared to previous methods is fine-tuning on a large-scale dataset of gene expression outliers created using a custom outlier detection pipeline. This fine-tuning process, designed to achieve robust performance on both unseen genes and unseen datasets, improves alignment of predictions with independent evidence from sequence conservation and mitigates challenges in predicting the direction of effect for regulatory motifs. Given that the current PromoterAI model is constrained by the relatively modest number of gene expression measurements available for training, our findings likely capture only a fraction of the potential impact of promoter variants. Future work leveraging expanded datasets may help identify additional variants, including those with tissue-specific effects or those located further away from the TSS that current models cannot predict accurately. Identifying disease genes sensitive to overexpression outliers could further increase the number of rare disease cases that can be solved by promoter variants. Additionally, characterizing each gene’s range of tolerance for expression variability is a key step toward bridging the gap between expression change and pathogenicity, enabling a more comprehensive identification of pathogenic promoter variation (77). Moreover, conservation of sequence elements in the human genome and that of closely related species suggests that other types of non-coding elements may also contribute to rare genetic diseases (78), including distal enhancers, 3′ and 5′ UTRs, and non-coding RNAs, all of which are critical in regulating gene expression (79–81). Mounting evidence indicates that the role of variation undetected by short-read sequencing in rare genetic diseases warrants closer investigation (82–84). These findings underscore substantial gaps in our understanding of how expression changes mediated by non-coding elements contribute to disease. Resolving these complexities will help unlock the full potential of the non-coding genome for diagnostic and therapeutic applications (85–87).
Materials and methods
PromoterAI training and fine-tuning Training dataset
We retrieved 502 bigWigs, covering Histone ChIP-seq, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq, and TF ChIP-seq assays from the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) portal (88–90) (https://www.encodeproject.org/). These bigWigs were selected to ensure high data quality and diversity across key experimental targets. Specifically, we excluded experiments flagged with audit issues, considered only one biological or technical replicate per experiment, and limited our selection to at most five experiments per target. For certain important targets with known relevance to promoter biology (TBP,
NFYA, NFYB, NFYC, SP1, YY1, CTCF, CTCFL, POLR2A, POLR2AphosphoS2, POLR2AphosphoS5, POLR2G, POLR2H, POLR2B, POLR3A, POLR3G, EP300, NELFE, BRD4, PAF1, EZH2, H3K36me3, H3K79me2, H3K79me1, H2AFZ, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, H4K5ac, and H4K20me1) (37, 47), no experiments met our strict filtering criteria. We permitted audit exceptions for these targets to guarantee their inclusion, resulting in a final list comprising 310 human and 192 mouse experiments. We downloaded ‘fold change over control’ bigWigs for experiments measuring histone modification or transcription factor binding, and ‘read-depth normalized signal’ bigWigs for those measuring accessibility. We sourced an additional 936 CAGE-seq bigWigs (468 per strand) from the Functional Annotation of the Mammalian Genome v5 (FANTOM5) portal (29) (https://fantom.gsc.riken.jp/5/datahub/). In particular, we downloaded strand-specific ‘CAGE tag starting site’ bigWigs for 188 human and 280 mouse experiments performed on tissues. To manage dynamic range and align scales, ENCODE bigWigs were transformed using f(x) = arcsinh(x), while FANTOM5 bigWigs were transformed using f(x) = arcsinh(1000x).
Model architecture
The input to the model is a nucleotide sequence of length 20,480, encoded as a matrix of size 20,480 × 4, with each nucleotide represented by a one-hot vector: A as [1, 0, 0, 0], C as [0, 1, 0, 0], G as [0, 0, 1, 0], and T as [0, 0, 0, 1]. The model outputs a matrix of size 4,096 × 970, representing predictions for 970 epigenetic and transcriptomic profiles (498 human and 472 mouse) across the central 4,096 input positions (fig. S1A). The input first passes through a fully connected layer to increase the channel dimension from 4 to 1,024, followed by 24 MetaFormer blocks. Each MetaFormer block consists of two parts: the first part includes batch normalization and a depthwise convolution layer with residual connection, and the second part includes batch normalization and a feed-forward network that increases the dimension by a factor of 4 and uses ReLU activation, also with residual connection. Each block has three hyper-parameters (C, W, D) corresponding to the number of input/output channels, convolution kernel size, and convolution dilation rate, respectively, effectively capturing features spanning (W - 1) × D nucleotides. The output of every fourth MetaFormer block passes through a fully connected shortcut layer with ReLU activation to adjust the channel dimension from 1,024 to 970, and the average of these outputs, followed by appropriate cropping, forms the final output. We set the kernel size to 5 throughout, which resulted in the model having ~208 million trainable parameters, and chose dilation rates such that the total feature coverage is 16,384 nucleotides. Model training
PromoterAI was trained to predict 970 epigenetic and strandspecific transcriptomic profiles at base-pair resolution. We focused exclusively on promoter regions, using a 4,096 bp window around each of the 244,939 GENCODE v39 and 81,540 GENCODE vM25 annotated TSS (92). Human chromosomes 1-20 and mouse chromosomes 1-19 were used for training the model, while human chromosomes 21-22 were reserved for determining early stopping. We trained the model for 100 epochs on 8 H100 GPUs, with the learning rate and weight decay following a schedule that included a 10-epoch linear warmup and a 10-epoch linear cool-down. Each epoch used a randomly chosen 10% subset of the training data. The batch size was set to 32 (4 per GPU), with each batch randomly selected from either human or mouse data and loss calculated only from the profiles of the chosen species. To increase data diversity, we randomly shifted TSS positions during sampling based on a truncated normal distribution (mean 0 and standard deviation 3,072). Additionally, we randomly chose the prediction strand for each gene, favoring the sense strand with a 3:1 ratio over the antisense strand. The best model was determined based on the lowest validation loss achieved during training.
Model fine-tuning
PromoterAI was subsequently fine-tuned on promoter variants with known expression consequences. To this end, we started with a comprehensive list of 218,832 GTEx rare promoter variants, each with expression effects calculated from RNA-seq data across multiple tissues (table S2; details provided in the section below). To concentrate on variants that modulate expression mainly via promoter mechanisms, we excluded those located within coding sequence (cdsStart cdsEnd) of any GENCODE v39 transcript or with SpliceAI score greater than 0.05, as coding and splice variants can often have expression consequences due to mechanisms like nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) and mRNA/protein stability alteration. Finally, we only selected variants that belonged to genes with at least one significant expression-altering variant (under- or overexpression p < 0.01, described in the section below). These filtering steps narrowed the list down to 57,795 variants. For each variant, we obtained two input nucleotide sequences from the sense strand, one for reference and another for alternate allele, each of length 20,480 centered around the variant. Both sequences were processed by identical copies of
the model, and the average difference between the profile predictions of the two copies across all positions and channels was calculated. The fully connected layers connecting the various MetaFormer blocks to the output were fine-tuned (~3 million parameters) to minimize MSE between this average and the known expression consequence (z-score). We used variants from odd chromosomes between 1-20 to fine-tune the model, while variants from chromosomes 21-22 were used for determining early stopping. The other settings for fine-tuning were identical to those of the initial training phase, except that no data augmentation or learning rate schedule was used.
Model ensemble
We trained and fine-tuned two PromoterAI models, one using only human data and the other using both human and mouse data.
Variant score
For each variant, we extracted two nucleotide sequences of length 20,480 centered around the variant on the sense strand, one for reference and another for alternate allele. The difference in their predictions (alt – ref), averaged across output positions (4,096 nucleotides) and channels, was used as the variant score. For each variant, the average of the scores from the two models that formed the ensemble was reported as the PromoterAI score.
GTEx multi-tissue expression outliers Promoter variants
We used RNA-seq and WGS data from the GTEx v8 release, with the generation of these data described in (30) and accessed via the Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP) portal (93) (study accession phs000424.v9.p2; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/gap/cgibin/study.cgi?study_id=phs000424.v9.p2). In order to identify promoter variants for inclusion in expression outlier testing, we intersected PASS variants from the GTEx v8 VCF with all protein-coding TSS +/− 500 bp positions, as defined by the GENCODE v39 GTF (https://www.gencodegenes.org/human/release_39.html), and then filtered to variants with allele frequency (AF) < 0.5% (restricted to singletons for analyses in Fig. 1, B to F) and located in the promoter region of the protein-coding transcript per gene with the most support from CAGE-seq across tissues. To select this transcript, we took the average read count across all tissues and cell types with CAGE-seq data available from FANTOM5 and selected the annotated transcript start site with the highest read count and used that transcript start site plus a 500 bp window both up and downstream as the promoter region for this gene. Generation of corrected expression z-scores across tissues
We restricted our analyses to the 49 tissues with at least 70 samples available with RNA-seq data. Within each tissue, we began with the gene-level transcripts per million (TPM) quantification from RNASeQC v1.1.9 (https://github.com/francois-a/rnaseqc) and log-transformed the expression values before scaling those values by gene and individual, after filtering for genes with a minimum TPM > 0.1 and read count > 6 in at least 20% of samples, per (30). We filtered to autosomal protein-coding genes only. To account for unmeasured technical or other factors influencing gene expression measurements, we corrected the resulting expression z-scores within each tissue for five genotype principal components (PCs), sex, and 30 expression PCs (available from the GTEx portal: https://gtexportal.org/home/downloads/adult-gtex/qtl) by fitting a linear model predicting scaled expression values from these factors and subtracting the predicted component. The resulting corrected values were re-scaled within tissue by both gene and individual (the enrichment of singleton promoter variants at this step shown in the top bar of Fig. 1B). Next, we applied further correction by subtracting the gene expression values predicted by up to 5 cis-eQTLs within 1 Mb of the TSS, starting from the eQTL significant variantgene pair summary statistics produced by (30), as these were largely common variants with weaker effects on gene expression than expected by rare variants. For all significant ciseQTLs identified by (30) within range, we assessed the Pearson correlation of genotypes with our corrected expression values and starting from the most significant variant, if the correlation was nominally significant at p < 0.01, we fit a linear model predicting expression from the cis-eQTL genotype and subtracted the predicted expression values from the observed value. We repeated this process until no significantly correlated cis-eQTLs remained, or until a maximum of 5 variants were included in the correction. The corrected values were then re-scaled across genes and individuals within tissue (the enrichment of singleton promoter variants at this step shown in the middle bar of Fig. 1B). Finally, to account for the influence of trans-factors and gene regulatory programs on gene expression, we trained a neural network to predict the expression of genes on one chromosome from the expression of genes on all other chromosomes as input, restricting to autosomes. All samples across all tissues were included in the model. To avoid overfitting, we randomly split these 15,201 samples (tissue by individual) in half and trained two models, using each to
predict the expression values in the other sample set. We then subtracted those predicted expression values from the observed expression values and re-scaled within each tissue to generate our final expression z-scores per individual, gene, and tissue instance (table S2; the enrichment of singleton promoter variants at this step shown in the bottom bar of Fig. 1B). The model consisted of one fully connected hidden layer of size 1,024 and was trained using an MSE loss with batch size of 32, patience of 20, dropout rate of 0.1, and normal initialization of model weights. The model was trained for a maximum of 100 epochs and was implemented in TensorFlow v2.3.0. To assess the impact of instances where predicted gene expression from this model (including the ciseQTL and trans-expression corrections) greatly deviated from the observed z-score (averaged across measured tissues per individual), we calculated the odds that an individual with an observed – predicted mean z-score (Δz-score) within a given range carried a promoter singleton as compared to individuals with Δz-scores not in that range. We constructed a 2 × 2 contingency table with rows corresponding to carrying a promoter singleton or not and columns indicating whether the individual’s Δz-score for the gene falls between [start, end). We reported the resulting odds ratios across Δz-score bins ranging from [-inf, -4) and [5, inf), with intermediate bins each comprising one Δz-score unit (Fig. 1C).
Expression outlier calling and enrichments
To identify expression outliers, for each promoter variant and gene combination, we took the vector of corrected z-scores across tissues from the carrier individual and a vector of control expression values from all non-carrier individuals from the same set of tissues as measured in the carrier. For nonsingleton cases, we concatenated the expression vectors across all carriers. We then performed a t-test between the two expression vectors to obtain a p-value for that variant’s effect and considered the average z-score across tissues in the carrier as an estimate of the effect size as well as direction. To determine the enrichment of true positive effect variants in a given outlier set obtained using a given p-value threshold, we defined a background expectation of the number of significant variants at that threshold by shuffling the variants across individuals and repeating the test. We then took the number of real observed significant variants at that threshold divided by the number of shuffled variants observed at the same significance level in the background. When shuffling, we randomly reassigned variant sets by sampling a background individual for each original individual. We calculated these enrichments for variants with p < 1e-4 (t-test) for either over- or under-expression at varying distance bins from each protein-coding gene’s TSS, considering variants in sliding windows of 100 bp in length every 10 bp from 5,000 bp upstream of the TSS to 5,000 bp downstream, averaging

To compare other approaches measuring expression outlier effects, we downloaded the previously generated ANEVADOT (33) scores and median expression z-scores (32) from the GTEx portal (https://gtexportal.org/home/downloads/adultgtex/additional_gtex_datasets) and the OUTRIDER R package (https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/OUT RIDER.html) (31). For OUTRIDER, we used the read counts from GTEx tissue samples as inputs for OUTRIDER v1.99.0. The OUTRIDER function ‘filterExpression’ was used to remove genes with 0 counts in all samples, followed by the ‘OUTRIDER’ function which performs the full OUTRIDER pipeline including an autoencoder-based correction for confounders. We confirmed that using this gene filtering approach vs the filtering approach described above did not impact the results and restricted to the same set of gene-variant pairs for the t-test comparison (though not for ANEVADOT, as it had many missing values). To calculate enrichments across each method, we set a threshold either on the median p-value for ANEVA-DOT, the median expression zscore, the t-test p-value when applied on our corrected zscores, or the t-test p-value when applied on the OUTRIDER autoencoder-corrected z-scores that resulted in 1,000, 500, and 100 significant hits within each method after shuffling variants across individuals. We then compared the number of real significant variants at those thresholds for each method and threshold (Fig. 1E). While OUTRIDER was not designed for this multi-tissue use case, we did want to confirm that our iterative correction steps outperformed an existing autoencoder model to account for non-promoter sequence factors, but different corrections and tests may be optimal for a single tissue analysis or for other variant categories or regions. To assess the average allelic effect per variant, within each tissue, we used the closest measured allelic expression single nucleotide polymorphism (aeSNP) to the gene’s TSS to calculate a reference ratio for each gene-individual that carries a rare promoter variant included in the outlier test, and then inverted the reference ratio if the aeSNP was carried on a different allele than the rare promoter variant, using the SHAPEIT2 phased genotypes from GTEx (30). To create the GTEx outlier benchmark, we focused on even chromosomes between 1-20, ensuring that they were not used during fine-tuning. Variants that meet these criteria were classified as under-expression outliers if they had an under-expression p < 1e-4 (206 variants), and overexpression outliers if overexpression p < 1e-4 (161 variants). Motif enrichments
We used the FIMO tool from the MEME Suite (https://memesuite.org/meme/index.html) (96) to identify sequence motifs overlapping GTEx singleton promoter variants. Our analysis focused on variants within TSS +/− 100 bp, excluding those located within coding sequence of any GENCODE v39 transcript or with a SpliceAI score greater than 0.05. We scanned within 15 bp of each variant on both strands using reference and alternate alleles, retaining matches with FIMO p < 1e-4. To reduce redundancy, we employed a curated list of 186 clustered motifs from (https://www.vierstra.org/resources/motif_clustering) (46) and only retained variants where the motif match was stronger on the reference allele. For each motif, we counted the number of variants with matches in over- and under-expression outliers as well as in controls. We then performed a Fisher’s exact test to determine motif enrichments for overand under-expression outliers compared to controls, ranking motifs by significance (Fig. 2B). Only motifs with at least ten
variant matches were considered.
In-silico motif insertion
We randomly sampled 50 loci within TSS +/− 500 bp for each of the 19,296 canonical protein-coding genes. At these loci, we inserted motifs that were enriched among under- and overexpression outliers (Fig. 2B) and 5 controls (random sequences), and calculated the predicted change in PromoterAI scores. For each motif, we aggregated the effects across genes and compared them with controls at various TSS distances (fig. S2B). We repeated this analysis using PromoterAI models before and after fine-tuning. Direction prediction accuracy was defined as the percentage of genes showing a positive score change for motifs enriched among under-expression outliers and a negative score change for motifs enriched among overexpression outliers (fig. S2E). To avoid saturation effects, for this analysis, we split the genes into two halves based on their average expression across GTEx tissues, inserting motifs enriched among under-expression outliers into the lower-expressed group and motifs enriched among overexpression outliers into the higher-expressed group.
Motif strengthening vs weakening
Motifs were classified into four categories based on gene annotations and Gene Ontology (GO) terms (97) using the mygene v3.2.2 Python package. Specifically, we searched for keywords ‘activator’, ‘activation’, ‘repressor’, and ‘repression’, and categorized motifs as either associated with only activating terms, only repressive terms, mainly activating with some repressive terms, or mainly repressive with some activating terms. For each variant, we calculated the difference in motif strength, measured as the difference in FIMO negative log pvalue for the overlapping motif between the reference and alternate sequences. We plotted the distributions of these differences for variants overlapping motifs with only activating or only repressive terms (Fig. 2C and table S4), and for variants overlapping motifs with both activating and repressive terms, sub-categorized based on their relative proportions (fig. S2C).

gnomAD variants
We downloaded the r3.0 VCF file from the gnomAD website (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/downloads) and focused only on variants marked with PASS in the FILTER column. We then filtered for variants labeled as nonsense, missense, or synonymous in the INFO column. For each variant type, we counted the number of singletons and those with AF > 0.1%. We constructed a 2 × 2 contingency table, with rows corresponding to nonsense or synonymous variants and columns corresponding to singleton or common variants. The odds ratio (OR) was calculated, and the depletion percentage was determined using the formula (1 – 1 / OR) × 100. We repeated this analysis using missense variants to obtain their depletion percentage. We obtained PromoterAI scores for all variants within TSS +/− 500 bp of canonical protein-coding genes. To calculate the depletion for a given PromoterAI score, we constructed a 2 × 2 contingency table, with the first row corresponding to variants with PromoterAI scores within 0.125 of the given score, second row corresponding to variants with PromoterAI scores between -0.05 and 0.05, and columns corresponding to singleton or common variants. The odds ratio of this contingency table was used to determine the depletion percentage at the given score (Fig. 3A). The displayed p-values were calculated using a chi-squared test on the contingency table. We repeated this analysis, focusing only on the subset of genes that met the required probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) criteria (Fig. 3B). To estimate the number of deleterious variants at a given TSS distance, we first calculated the odds ratio using the same procedure, with the first row corresponding to variants with PromoterAI score > 0.1 for overexpression and < -0.1 for under-expression, only counting variants that were within 5 bp of the given TSS distance. We then calculated the number of deleterious variants for each TSS distance as the number of singletons with PromoterAI score > 0.1 for overexpression and < -0.1 for under-expression, multiplied by the depletion factor (1 – 1 / OR) (Fig. 3C).
